Summary

TCGA-LUAD: Lung Adenocarcinoma (mutations, 200 patients), 200 samples was analysed with the Somatic mutations and copy number workflow (version 1.0.0) on the LSMA Analysis Lab. To describe how the samples group by 'vital_status'. In summary, the stages completed and their outputs are below. 3 point(s) are flagged under Limitations and should be read before the results are used.

Introduction

From annotated somatic mutations of a group of tumours (a MAF file) to quality control, the landscape of mutated genes, mutational signatures, comparison of patient groups and copy-number changes. Human samples. Variant calling and annotation are done before the data reaches this workflow. The data analysed here is of kind 'mutations'.

Aim

To describe how the samples group by 'vital_status'.

Source: TCGA project TCGA-LUAD (Lung Adenocarcinoma), open-access files from the NCI Genomic Data Commons. Somatic mutations called against each patient's normal tissue by the GDC's pipelines (open-access, masked MAF files, GRCh38), with the copy-number segments of the same patients' tumours. 200 of 559 patients; 61,301 mutations. Copy-number segments (SNP array, DNAcopy, masked) for 196 of them. https://portal.gdc.cancer.gov/projects/TCGA-LUAD Cite the TCGA Research Network and the marker paper of this project.

Methods

Assembled from what each completed stage recorded. Check it against the parameter tables below before using it in a write-up.

Somatic mutations of 200 samples were read from TCGA-LUAD_mutations.maf.gz (hg38 (GRCh38)): 46,416 protein-changing mutations in 12,793 genes. Variant calling and annotation were done before the data reached the platform.

Filters on read support: none (the mutations are used as supplied). Tumour mutational burden was expressed per megabase assuming 38 Mb of sequenced coding region.

Genes were ranked by the share of all 200 samples with a protein-changing mutation (maftools). Pairs of frequently mutated genes were tested for co-occurrence and mutual exclusivity: Fisher's exact test per gene pair (maftools::somaticInteractions), Benjamini-Hochberg adjusted.

Mutational signatures: 96 sequence contexts (maftools::trinucleotideMatrix); refit to COSMIC v3.2 signatures (MutationalPatterns::fit_to_signatures_strict), using BSgenome.Hsapiens.UCSC.hg38; samples with at least 50 substitutions were also fitted individually.

Mutation frequencies were compared between groups (Dead vs Alive; 82 and 115 samples): Fisher's exact test per gene (genes selected with maftools::mafCompare), with group sizes from the sample sheet, for genes mutated in at least 5 samples, adjusted with the BH method.

Copy-number segments of 196 samples were summarised in 2 Mb bins: a gain was a log2 ratio of at least 0.2, a loss at most -0.2. Frequency of gains and losses from segment log2 ratios (no statistical test of recurrence; GISTIC is not run).

Random seed: 42. Software: R 4.5.2; Bioconductor 3.21; BSgenome.Hsapiens.UCSC.hg38 1.4.5; GenomeInfoDb 1.44.3; MutationalPatterns 3.18.0; TxDb.Hsapiens.UCSC.hg38.knownGene 3.21.0; data.table 1.18.6.1; maftools 2.24.0.

Analyses were run on the LSMA Analysis Lab (workflow 'somatic-mutations' version 1.0.0).

Results

One section per stage, in the order they ran. The badge on each heading says how far its output can be taken: exploratory output describes the data, statistically supported output carries a test, and interpretation is a reading of either.

Stage 1 of 6

Data input Exploratory

A somatic mutation is a change in the DNA of the tumour that the patient's normal cells do not have. After sequencing tumour and normal tissue, a variant caller (for example Mutect2) lists these changes and an annotation tool (VEP, ANNOVAR, Funcotator) works out which gene each one hits and what it does to the protein. The result for a whole group of patients is a MAF file: one row per mutation, with the gene, the position, the kind of change and the sample. This stage reads it, together with a sample sheet describing the patients and, optionally, copy-number segments.

Stage 2 of 6

Variant quality control Exploratory

The mutations are counted per sample and sorted by kind (missense, nonsense, frameshift, splice site, ...) and by type (single-base substitution, insertion, deletion). If the file holds read counts, the share of reads carrying each mutation (variant allele fraction) is shown and can be used as a filter. The tumour mutational burden is the number of protein-changing mutations per megabase sequenced.

Note. Flagged sample(s) with far more mutations than the rest: TCGA-05-4382. They dominate gene frequencies and signatures; check whether they are hypermutated tumours or a technical problem.
Note. 1 sample(s) have no protein-changing mutation. They count as unmutated in every frequency.

How to interpret this stage

Expect C>T to be the commonest substitution. Samples flagged for very many mutations may be genuinely hypermutated (defective DNA repair, strong mutagen exposure) or technical failures; either way they dominate every summary and deserve a decision. Formalin-fixed samples show an excess of C>T at low allele fraction.

How to interpret this stage

In acute myeloid leukaemia expect FLT3, NPM1 and DNMT3A at the top, often together, and each in a quarter of patients or fewer. Look at the kind of mutation: one recurrent change (NPM1 frameshift insertions) suggests a gain of a specific function, scattered truncating mutations suggest loss of function. Treat the pair tests as statistically supported only after correction for the number of pairs.

Stage 4 of 6

Mutational signatures Biological interpretation

Each single-base substitution is sorted into one of 96 types by the change itself and the base on either side. Processes that mutate DNA, such as ageing, ultraviolet light, tobacco smoke or faulty repair, each leave a characteristic profile over these 96 types, called a mutational signature. The observed profile is expressed as a mixture of the known signatures of the COSMIC catalogue.

Key numbers

Method96 sequence contexts (maftools::trinucleotideMatrix); refit to COSMIC v3.2 signatures (MutationalPatterns::fit_to_signatures_strict)
Reference genomeBSgenome.Hsapiens.UCSC.hg38
Substitutions in cohort59,376

Median substitutions per sample211
Samples fitted individually169
Min substitutions per sample50
Cohort reconstruction cosine0.984

What this stage found

This stage recorded substitutions in cohort: 59,376, samples with substitutions: 199, samples fitted individually: 169 and cohort reconstruction cosine: 0.984.

This is shown in Figure 10, Figure 11 and Figure 12.

How to interpret this stage

Signatures 1 and 5 accumulate with age and appear in almost every cancer. Tobacco (4), ultraviolet light (7), APOBEC enzymes (2, 13) and repair defects (3, 6) are the classic specific ones. Small contributions from many signatures are a sign of overfitting. The cosine similarity states how well the mixture reproduces the observed profile.

Parameters used

Analyse mutational signatures (enabled)yesdefault
Substitutions a sample needs to be analysed by itself (min_substitutions_per_sample)50default
Strictness of the fit (max_delta)0.004default

Comparison of patient groups Statistically supported

For every gene mutated in enough patients, the number of mutated and unmutated patients is compared between two groups with Fisher's exact test, and the p-values are corrected for the number of genes tested.

Note. No gene differs between the groups after correction for multiple testing. With groups of this size only very large differences can be detected.

How to interpret this stage

A gene with a small adjusted p-value is mutated at a different frequency in the two groups. In the leukaemia demonstration data, NPM1 mutations are absent from acute promyelocytic leukaemia (0 of 21 patients) and found in a fifth of the others, yet the difference does not survive correction for the 22 genes tested: a lesson in what 21 patients can and cannot show. With small groups, only large differences can be detected, and absence of a significant gene is not evidence that the groups are alike.

Stage 6 of 6

Copy-number changes Exploratory

Tumours gain and lose whole chromosomes, arms or smaller pieces. Tools such as CNVkit compare the read depth of the tumour with normal tissue along the genome and cut it into segments, each with a log2 ratio: zero for the normal two copies, positive for a gain, negative for a loss. This stage counts, for every stretch of the genome, in how many samples it is gained or lost.

Key numbers

MethodFrequency of gains and losses from segment log2 ratios (no statistical test of recurrence; GISTIC is not run)

What this stage found

This stage recorded number of samples: 196, segments used: 45,302, gain log2: 0.2, loss log2: -0.2, bin mb: 2 and median fraction genome altered: 0.2359.

This is shown in Figure 14 and Figure 15.

How to interpret this stage

Tall, broad peaks are arm-level or whole-chromosome events; narrow tall peaks point at single genes. Compare with what is known for the cancer type. Acute myeloid leukaemia has a quiet genome with few changes (losses on chromosomes 5 and 7, gain of 8); many solid tumours are altered across most of the genome.

Discussion

What the run amounts to, drawn from the stages that carry a judgement. Every sentence below was written by the stage that reached it; none is a later interpretation.

This run describes the data rather than testing a hypothesis about it, so there is no verdict to draw together here. The Results describe what was measured.

The run raised 3 warnings, listed with the stages that raised them. They are part of the result, not notes beside it.
